title: The CV that actually gets read in 2026
excerpt: Recruiters spend under a minute on a first pass. Here is what survives the skim — and what gets you filtered out before a human ever looks.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: A CV has one job: earn the conversation. It is not your biography, and it is not read the way you wrote it. On a first pass — human or automated — it is skimmed for role fit, recency and evidence. Optimise for the skim and the read takes care of itself.

Lead with a three-line profile that names the role you do, the level you operate at and the thing you are demonstrably good at. Skip the adjectives; 'Management accountant, CIMA finalist, month-end owner for a £40m division' beats any amount of 'dynamic self-starter'.

For each role, one line of context (company, what it does, your remit) then three to five bullets of evidence. Numbers survive skimming: budgets owned, revenue influenced, time saved, error rates cut. If you cannot quantify, name the artefact — the process you built, the report leadership relies on.

Keep it to two pages, save it as a PDF with your name in the filename, and mirror the vocabulary of the listing — not to game software, but because the person reading is checking your world matches theirs. Then let the CV rest and write the application answers fresh: on Orbit Jobs, direct-apply roles put your answers in front of the employer alongside the CV, and specific beats polished every time.

title: Salary negotiation: the UK playbook
excerpt: Most UK candidates never counter. A calm, scripted ask raises offers more often than it risks them — here is the script.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: British discomfort with talking about money costs real salary. Employers expect a counter; most budget for one. The candidates who ask, calmly and with evidence, are not remembered as difficult — they are remembered as people who know their market.

Do the work before the offer. Note the advertised range on every comparable listing (the disclosed-salary filter on Orbit Jobs exists for exactly this), and anchor to the top half of the evidence, not to your current salary. Your current pay is where you have been; the range is where the market is.

When the offer comes, thank them, ask for a day, and return with one number and one reason: 'I'm keen to accept — with the scope we discussed, I was expecting closer to £X, based on the range for comparable roles. Can we get there?' Then stop talking. Silence is the negotiation.

If the base cannot move, trade deliberately: start date, review at six months in writing, study support, additional leave, remote days. Get whatever is agreed into the offer letter. And if the answer is a flat no with no path — that is information about the next three years, not just the first month.

title: The eight interview questions that repeat — and how to answer them
excerpt: Across fields and levels, UK interviews recycle the same core questions. Prepare these eight stories and you have covered most of the hour.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: Interviews feel unpredictable but rarely are. 'Tell me about yourself' opens most of them: give ninety seconds — present role, one proof point, why this job. It is a warm-up, not a life story; its only function is to make the next question easy.

The middle of the hour is competency territory: a time you led without authority, a conflict you resolved, a mistake you own, a result you are proud of. Prepare four stories with the same skeleton — situation in one line, what you did in three, result with a number — and you can flex them to almost any phrasing. Write them down; rehearsed-once beats improvised-live.

'Why do you want this role?' is answered with their words, not yours: the listing told you what they care about, so connect your evidence to it explicitly. And when they ask what questions you have, ask about the work ('what does the first ninety days look like?', 'what separates good from great in this seat?') — the questions you ask are scored as hard as the answers you give.

title: Notice periods, counter-offers and leaving well
excerpt: What UK notice actually obliges you to do, how buy-outs work, and why the counter-offer statistics are so brutal.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: Your notice period is contract, not law — statutory minimums are shorter than most contracts specify. Check the document, not the folklore: many 'three month' beliefs turn out to be one month on paper. Gardening leave and payment in lieu are the employer's options, not yours, but both are negotiable at exit.

New employers routinely wait eight to twelve weeks for the right hire, and some will buy notice out. Say your notice honestly in applications — on Orbit Jobs it is an optional profile field precisely because it changes conversations — and never resign until the written offer is in your inbox.

On counter-offers: the folk statistic that most acceptors leave within a year survives because the underlying logic is sound. The counter fixes the salary and leaves the reasons. Take it only if money was genuinely the whole problem. Either way, resign kindly, work your notice properly and hand over well — UK industries are small villages, and the manager you leave today interviews you somewhere else in five years.

title: Remote, hybrid, 'flexible': decoding what listings actually mean
excerpt: Work-model words are doing heavy lifting in UK job ads. Here is how to read them — and the questions that surface the truth.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: On Orbit Jobs, work model is a structured field — on-site, hybrid or remote — because the words in ad copy have gone soft. 'Flexible working' can mean anything from full autonomy to one work-from-home Friday a month. Structured filters beat adjectives.

Hybrid is now the UK default for office roles, typically two or three anchor days. The questions that matter at interview: which days, who decides, and is it policy or team custom? Custom evaporates with a reorganisation; policy survives one.

Remote deserves equal scrutiny in the other direction: is it remote-first (processes assume distribution) or remote-tolerated (meetings happen in a room you are not in)? Ask how decisions get documented and when the team last met in person. And check the map: some 'remote UK' roles carry a quarterly on-site expectation that quietly assumes you live within two hours of one city.

title: Write job ads people actually answer
excerpt: Employers: your ad is competing with every listing in the search results. Salary, specifics and a human voice are the whole game.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: A job ad is not a job description. The internal JD lists duties for HR; the ad sells one decision — 'this is worth twenty minutes of my evening'. Write it for the skim: what the job is, what it pays, where it happens, why your team, in that order.

Publish the salary range. On Orbit Jobs, listings with a disclosed range are what candidates filter for; 'competitive' reads as 'below the range you are imagining' and silently removes you from the shortlists of exactly the experienced people you want. If the range is wide, say what moves someone through it.

Cut requirements to the real bar. Every 'must have' beyond about six halves your applicant pool, and evidence says it disproportionately deters strong candidates who self-filter honestly. Separate must from nice explicitly. Then close with a process promise — stages, timescale, who they will meet — and keep it. The single biggest driver of application abandonment is silence after apply; our three-question screening beats a covering letter for signal anyway.

title: Three screening questions beat fifty CV filters
excerpt: The highest-signal, lowest-effort improvement to your pipeline is asking a small number of specific questions at apply.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: CVs tell you where someone has been; screening questions tell you how they think about your problem. When you post a role on Orbit Jobs you can add up to three questions to the apply form — used well, they compress your first interview stage into the application itself.

Ask about the work, not the person: 'Describe a month-end you ran solo — what broke and what did you change?' outperforms 'Why do you want this job?' every time. One question testing the core skill, one testing judgement, one practical (notice, right-to-work, base expectations) is a complete set. More than three measurably cuts completion.

Read answers before CVs — it de-biases the pass and surfaces career-changers with the right thinking. Two-line answers to one-line questions are signal. So are answers that quietly correct the question's assumption: interview those people first.

title: Your first 90 days: run them like a project
excerpt: The probation period is mutual. A simple three-phase plan turns new-job anxiety into visible early wins.
author: Orbit Jobs Editorial
body: Weeks one to four are for listening: map who decides, who influences and who quietly runs everything. Book the introductions yourself instead of waiting for them to be arranged, and keep a running list of everything that confuses you — it is your freshest, shortest-lived asset, and half of it will turn out to confuse everyone.

Weeks five to eight, ship something small but visible: the report nobody had time to fix, the process with one step too many. Early wins are chosen, not assigned — pick one your manager's manager will notice, deliver it properly, and say plainly what you did.

Weeks nine to twelve, ask for the mid-probation conversation before it is offered: what is working, what should change, what would 'exceeding' look like by month six? Write the answers down and send them back as a summary. People who do this stop being 'the new hire' a month earlier — and if the answers are vague or shifting, that is early information worth having too.
